title: The Unconscious of Political Systems: A Theory of Psychopolitical Structures
abstract: ABSTRACT Political systems do more than distribute power and resources. They also shape how anxiety, desire, aggression, dependency, loss, and trauma are interpreted and managed. Psychoanalytic political theory offers many concepts for these processes, but they are often developed within separate traditions. This article proposes a functional framework of seven psychopolitical structures: generative, figurative, cathectic, defensive, institutionalizing, recursive‐temporal, and transformative. The categories identify different functions rather than equivalent kinds of phenomena. Together they show how diffuse psychic pressures acquire political meaning, affective force, institutional durability, and historical continuity. The framework does not treat societies as patients or reduce politics to individual psychology. Instead, it examines how narratives, identifications, defenses, institutions, and memories organize collective responses to uncertainty and conflict. These structures interact recursively and can stabilize around three ideal‐typical attractors: projective closure, adaptive containment, and reflexive reworking. Projective closure turns contradiction outward into enemyhood. Adaptive containment manages distress while leaving many of its political sources intact. Reflexive reworking keeps anxiety, implication, loss, and institutional defense open to interpretation and revision. The article argues that democratic psychopolitical capacity lies not in eliminating unconscious conflict but in making its political organization more contestable, responsible, and revisable.
